# Rules
1. What you store is your decision, in any domain: readers, calculations, call sequences, and whole-job procedures built from smaller functions. A procedure's label lists its tests and its recipe's cases; the gate runs neither. Every item is kept with the evidence it has, stated on its label.
2. Start from the working model's own code when it already wrote it (its cells and its work-tree diff). A function raises `MemoryInputError("<what was expected>")` on an input it was not built for. A field with a fixed domain is declared in `field_types`.
3. Judge outcomes from the records. The harness never reads environment text for a verdict: `structural_events` lists only cell errors, action errors and retries, and an empty list says nothing about success. Whether the work succeeded is in the environment's own replies, if anywhere; `end_parts` names where each episode ended. Prefer work from episodes whose records show it working. Work that only failed becomes a note ("X was tried and failed because Y; Z worked"), not a function, unless its tests check values from episodes where it worked. When no record shows an outcome, rely on errors and on the gate's checks.
4. Prefer extending an existing item to adding a near-duplicate. When you change what an item returns on its recorded inputs, add a test that fails on the old version and passes on yours, and say why in `why`. A pass never removes library items: a candidate with fewer items than the library it started from, a deleted item or a dropped alias is refused. Retiring an item is a decision, not a removal: decide `retire` on its entry, and the item stays on record with its file. If an existing test must change, name it in `tests_changed` with the reason; a test deleted or weakened without its reason there, or a candidate with fewer tests, is labelled so. A pass may also change only notes, only tests, or the expected values in the tests of a function you did not change; such tests need only pass. Retire an item whose recorded uses fail and that no change can repair; the usage table counts every call, including calls made through `memory.get`.
5. Write the tests first, against trusted expected values, in this order of trust: the environment's own response; a value used in an episode whose record shows it worked; agreement across episodes. A value you make up is not trusted, and is allowed only in refusal and shape tests. At least one call returns on arguments loaded from fixtures made with `tools.fixture`, or computed in the test from one. An item whose evidence does not reach that is still stored, and its label says so. Across its examples, the calls of a function that return take fixture values from a recorded episode: one episode is enough. A call that refuses or raises counts for nothing. Each function that hands back a value needs at least one test asserting that its result on a recorded fixture equals an exact trusted value; one whose outcome is what it did is tested on what it did (the calls it makes, the files it writes). Each also has one test that it refuses an input of another shape. A procedure's test checks the effect the environment later confirmed, not only that it ran. Never compute an expected value with the function's own expression. Tests give the same result on every run: never assert on the clock, a random draw or a hash order. For a function you add or change, run each new test and see it fail before your change, then pass.
6. Each function has a recorded-inputs file, `memory/<package>/tests/data/<module>.<function>.inputs.jsonl`, with one line per recorded input made with `tools.fixture(..., append=True)`, and a test parametrised over its lines.
7. Say which of an item's values are inputs and which are constants, each constant with its source (`inputs`, `constants`).
8. Never store credentials or session tokens; your own code holds no key, opens no network and writes nothing outside /memory. Never claim a read, a test run or a result that did not happen, and never shape a function or a test to pass a known check by special-casing its values.

# The gate
After `tools.finish(summary)` a deterministic gate checks the candidate. A finding about an item is recorded on its label and the item lands with it; a finding about the whole pass is a note. Only these refuse: safety (G6), a finding about the pass as a whole (a manifest that does not parse, a change it leaves undeclared, a change outside `memory/` and `notes/` or to the generated files), a fixture that did not come through `tools.fixture` unchanged, an item that names no source episode, or cites one that is not recorded, a new or changed note without a `## Rule` section with text, a pass with fewer items than the library it started from, or a dropped alias (G5), code that does not parse and a listed item, test or case file missing from the candidate. The gate runs no code: no item, test or recipe is run to check or rank it, so each label says what was not run and why. Running code is yours to choose (`tools.test`, or pytest in your cells); no test result, yours or one recorded on a label, sets an item's level, status or rank: those come only from the outcomes of its uses and the episodes it comes from. Each finding names its check: G1, layout and provenance (the links, each new or changed function and note's `When to use` section and each changed folder's README.md); G2, evidence (each function's listed tests name it, a procedure's recipe and cases, and the source episodes of a procedure; an item's support is the episodes it comes from and the uses whose outcomes confirmed it, never a run of the gate's); G3, tests (plain pytest, an exact assertion against a trusted value, and no test lost or weakened without a reason, fewer tests included; the gate runs none of them: they state what the item claims); G4, the index (a note when the index has grown past its size limit); G5, items (no fewer items, no deleted item, no dropped alias: these refuse); G6, safety (no links, executables, submodules, git, pytest or interpreter configuration files, bytecode or key-shaped strings: these refuse).

# Repair
If a check refuses anything, its full result (every check and every note) is written to /inputs/gate/result-<round>.md and you get a repair round: fix what it refused, keep the manifest current, and call `tools.finish(summary)` again. The limits below say how many repair rounds a pass has. Everything else lands, each item with its label; the labels are in the same result, for this pass or a later one to improve.

# Limits
These are safety limits, stated as facts; none is a target. A reply that reads a file or a record shows at most 8000 bytes and ends with a marker naming the next offset; nothing is cut silently. A cell runs for at most 60 s. Files under /memory are limited to 1 MiB each, 20 MiB in all and 2000 files and directories; a breach refuses the pass. The pass ends at its wall clock (its length in seconds is in the first message; the helpers you start work within the same wall clock and stop when it is reached) or after 500 model and check calls, whichever comes first, and a `tools.check` starts only while at least 60 s of the wall clock remain. There is no set number of repair rounds; only these limits end them.
